title: Legal aid staff attorney
description: staff attorney at a civil legal aid organisation in the United States, representing low-income clients in housing, benefits and family matters

employer_types: Regional or statewide legal aid society
Medical-legal partnership housed in a hospital or clinic
Law school clinic affiliated legal services organization
company_sizes: Large urban or statewide program (200-500+ staff)
reports_to: Practice group director or unit director
Directing attorney of a branch office
Executive director or deputy director (in small offices)
depends_on_them: Low-income clients facing eviction, benefit terminations or family crises
Intake staff and hotline workers who route matters to them
Pro bono volunteer attorneys who take overflow cases
Law students and interns under their supervision
Medical-legal partnership clinicians and social workers who refer patients
Domestic violence advocates and community partners who refer clients
Funders and grant managers who rely on case-outcome and case-count reporting

summary: A staff attorney at a civil legal aid organisation represents income-eligible clients in housing (eviction defense, subsidized housing and voucher terminations, repairs), public benefits (SNAP, Medicaid, TANF, unemployment, SSI/SSDI) and family matters (protective orders, custody, support, guardianship). They review intake and notices, calendar short deadlines, gather documents, draft answers, fair hearing requests, petitions and stipulations, and appear in high-volume dockets and administrative hearings. They also negotiate settlements, follow up to ensure agencies actually restore benefits, supervise students and volunteers, refer out-of-scope matters, and work with social workers and advocates, all under heavy caseloads, limited funding, and funder eligibility rules.

sample_claims.statement: A matter begins when a client phones the central intake line or submits an online application, and an intake worker records the problem in the case management system, commonly LegalServer.
Intake staff check household income against the funder ceiling, usually 125 percent of the federal poverty guideline for Legal Services Corporation funded work, before a matter is accepted.
A conflict check runs against the case management database for adverse parties such as the landlord, the housing authority, or the other parent.
The attorney asks the client to photograph or bring every paper, including the notice, lease, summons, rent receipts, and any landlord ledger.
The attorney drafts an answer raising defenses such as defective notice, payment, retaliation, breach of the warranty of habitability, and discrimination.
Code inspectors can take weeks to schedule a visit, and the eviction hearing often arrives first.
The attorney checks whether the property is covered by the CARES Act thirty day notice requirement, for example through a federally backed mortgage or subsidy.
Eviction filings continue to appear on tenant screening reports even after dismissal, and clients keep being denied apartments.
On eviction docket days the attorney appears in a batch of thirty to forty cases and waits for each case to be called.
For a domestic violence survivor the attorney assembles VAWA protections, including the HUD certification form and an emergency transfer request.
Voucher holders have only sixty to one hundred twenty days to find a unit, and landlords who refuse vouchers make this hard to meet.
The attorney asks the court for a continuance while an assistance application is pending.
Attorneys keep direct email addresses for agency liaisons and advocate lines to bypass the public call center.
Because of immigrant eligibility restrictions the attorney verifies the immigration category before advising on benefits and sometimes refers the case to an immigration partner.
A supervising attorney reviews cases in weekly or biweekly meetings, and newer attorneys have pleadings reviewed before filing.
LSC-funded programs screen income against 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines, so working clients just above the line get turned away despite real need.
Landlord ledgers frequently lump late fees, repair charges, and utilities into rent, making the real balance hard to establish.
Code enforcement inspections can take weeks to schedule, and the report often arrives after the hearing.
When a benefits problem raises public charge or immigration concerns, attorneys refer the question to immigration specialists rather than handling it themselves.
Because LSC rules limit fee-generating cases, attorneys usually refer fee-eligible Social Security cases to private counsel unless the client cannot find anyone.
Pro bono coordinators place overflow cases with volunteer attorneys, and staff attorneys mentor them.
Staff attorneys supervise law school clinic students and interns on research and client interviews.
Attorneys lean on social workers and housing counselors to explain a client's situation and handle the non-legal needs.
Attorneys debrief with trusted colleagues after a hard hearing, often using dark humor.
Salaries well below private practice, combined with student loans, drive turnover, and attorneys regularly weigh leaving.
Attorneys use public service loan forgiveness and employer loan repayment assistance to stay in the job.
Pandemic eviction moratoria and emergency rental assistance expired, and eviction caseloads returned to or exceeded earlier levels.

Before a matter reaches the attorney, intake paralegals or hotline staff screen the caller's household income against the program's eligibility ceiling, typically around 125 percent of the federal poverty guidelines for LSC-funded programs.
When clients cannot come into the office, attorneys collect signatures through e-signature tools or by having the client photograph a signed page and text it back.

The attorney checks whether the property is federally backed or subsidized, using public databases of subsidized and tax-credit housing, because that affects notice periods and defenses such as the CARES Act 30-day notice requirement.

open_questions.question: Which problems come up most often in your caseload (nonpayment evictions, holdovers, subsidized-housing terminations, benefits cutoffs, DV-related family cases), and has the mix shifted recently?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Case mix determines which skills, forms and relationships matter most and differs by region and program.

open_questions.question: How many days do you typically have between service of the summons and the first hearing or answer deadline in your court, and how often is that really enough?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Actual timelines vary by state and county and drive triage and workload.

open_questions.question: What does a typical eviction docket day look like in your courthouse, including how many cases, where negotiations happen, and how much time you get with each client?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Docket practices vary widely and shape how much real lawyering is possible.

open_questions.question: How long do steps really take: code inspections, fair hearing scheduling, SSA hearings, GAL reports, housing authority file requests?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Actual delays versus official timelines affect strategy such as continuances and emergency requests.

open_questions.question: Which workarounds are tolerated or even encouraged in your office, such as texting clients, photographed signatures, or informal agency contacts?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Informal practices determine real efficiency and differ by supervisor and ethics guidance.

open_questions.question: How is the income eligibility line handled for clients just above 125 percent, and are there exceptions, other funding sources or referral options in your program?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Programs have different funders and waiver policies, changing who can actually be served.

open_questions.question: How much of your time goes to administrative work like e-filing problems, fee waivers, case notes and funder reporting?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Administrative burden is a major source of lost time and burnout.

open_questions.question: How do you decide between full representation, limited-scope help and brief advice when capacity runs out?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Triage criteria are informal and vary by office and funder priorities.

open_questions.question: What is your caseload, and how many hearings or deadlines are you juggling in a typical week?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Caseload size varies and affects quality of work and turnover.

open_questions.question: How reliable are pro bono volunteers and law students, and how often do you end up taking cases back?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The real value of volunteers depends on screening, training and supervision capacity.

open_questions.question: How do local clerks and judges differ in handling e-filing, fee waivers, interpreters and continuances, and how do you learn those quirks?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Local practice often outweighs written rules and is learned only by experience.

open_questions.question: Which agency contacts or liaisons are most valuable, and what happens when they leave or stop responding?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Relationship-based escalation channels are fragile and not documented anywhere.

open_questions.question: How often do clients go silent or miss hearings, and what works best to keep in touch?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Client loss is a major risk, and effective contact practices vary by population.

open_questions.question: How do you handle rental assistance applications that landlords or agencies push onto your office, and how much time does it take?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It shows hidden work outside core legal services that varies by locality.

open_questions.question: What supports keep you in the job (loan forgiveness, supervision, debriefing, EAP), and what would make you leave?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Retention factors differ across organisations and shape staffing and workplace design.
